appendix_d.text: 'Table A8 replicates Saiz' estimation for the 2000-2010 period using the same set of metros, specifications and variables. The average implied metro supply elasticity declines to 1.25 for 2000-2010, indicating that many metropolitan areas have become increasingly supply constrained over time.' Saiz' 1970-2000 estimates have a mean of 2.54 (s.d. 1.43) for the 237 metro regions of the BSH data, against 0.38-0.41 (s.d. 0.11) for BSH's metro-region aggregates of their tract elasticities.

elasticity_variants.definitions: college = householder with a bachelor's degree or more (YEARSCH >= 14) or an associate degree or more (YEARSCH >= 12); BFM's text does not define 'college degree or more' (their Table 1 has 44% of the heads of household of a census block group with a college degree or more, block-group average); children = a person under 18 in the household (R18UNDR); slopes are the linear projections Cov(x, income) / Var(income)

elasticity_with_college.assumptions: independent sampling errors of the Table 8 coefficients (their covariance is not published; income and college are positively correlated so it is likely negative, which would lower the SE of the sum); the other Table 8 interactions (children, race, work status, age) are held fixed; the college dummy changes by gamma per dollar of income, gamma = Cov(college, income) / Var(income) in the PUMS Bay Area households (linear projection), or the local slope of E[college | income] at $54,103 (logit, local linear window +-$20,000)

housing_share.definition: ratio of aggregates: aggregate shelter + utilities / aggregate total expenditures, CE 2018, consumer-unit weights (sum R H / sum Y' over adults in the model)
housing_share.basis: shelter + utilities / total expenditures, CE 2018; terciles of income before taxes built from the CE deciles (fractional weights; the quintile-based values are in the JSON)

recommended.model_definitions: Preferences (1 - aH) log c + aH log(H - hmin) over non-housing consumption c and housing H; Y' is the household's outlay on c and housing (income after taxes, education goods, moving, residence-charge and other fixed goods costs), C = Y' - R hmin the supernumerary expenditure. Then H = hmin + aH C / R, R H = R hmin + aH C, c = (1 - aH) C and Y' = C + R hmin (DESIGN_v2: the line of DESIGN.md M1b 'Y' = (1 + aH) C + R hmin' double counts aH C; it holds only for preferences log c + aH log(H - hmin), whose marginal housing share is aH / (1 + aH)). aH is the MARGINAL budget share of housing, the quantity estimated by the Stone-Geary fit s(y) = aH + (1 - aH) h / y; hmin is h over mean expenditure per equivalent adult (units of Cbar at R = 1). `housing_share` must be computed as a RATIO OF AGGREGATES, sum_i R H_i / sum_i Y'_i over the adults (and `housing_share_by_income` as the same ratio within terciles of pre-tax income): the CE targets are aggregate shelter + utilities over aggregate expenditures. A mean over adults of R H_i / Y'_i (M1B_SPEC) is a different moment: because the share falls with expenditure it is larger (the consumer-unit-weighted mean of the five CE quintile shares, 0.276, is a lower bound for a household-level mean of ratios, against the aggregate 0.258). Units: dollar amounts per household (r_car, the housing-cost gap) are divided by the mean expenditure per consumer unit, $61,224, as in housing_costs.md, which is unit-free if per-household costs and consumption scale together with household size; hmin is already a ratio of two amounts in the same unit (h per equivalent adult over mean expenditure per equivalent adult), so the dollar h per equivalent adult must not be divided by $61,224 (a household of mean size has h = hmin x $61,224).
